ai.definition: Synthetic biology applications in medicine leverage advanced biotechnological techniques to edit genes precisely and deliver drugs directly to target cells.
ai.howItWorks: Using advanced CRISPR tools, synthetic biology allows for highly targeted gene editing and the creation of engineered biological systems that can be used for drug delivery.
ai.problemSolved: Challenges in precise genetic modification and targeted drug delivery in medical treatments, including off-target effects and limited efficacy.
ai.manufacturing: Involves the design and construction of biological parts, devices, and systems using standard and semi-standard components.
ai.buildProcess: Design, build, test, and learn (DBTL) cycles are used to iteratively develop synthetic biology constructs for medical applications.
ai.costDrivers: High initial research costs, complex regulatory compliance, and the need for specialized equipment and expertise.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected growth as CRISPR technology matures and more clinical trials are conducted.
ai.regulation: Subject to rigorous oversight by regulatory bodies such as the FDA, with ongoing developments in guidelines and standards.
ai.risks: Safety concerns related to off-target effects, ethical considerations of gene editing, and potential environmental impacts from engineered organisms.
ai.profitability: Potential for high returns through novel treatments but faces significant barriers including R&D costs and regulatory hurdles.
ai.futureDevelopment: Ongoing research aims to improve CRISPR efficiency, expand therapeutic applications, and develop more robust delivery systems.

glossary.def: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats, a genetic engineering tool used for precise gene editing.
Messenger RNA, a molecule that carries instructions from DNA to the ribosomes in cells, where proteins are synthesized.
Small circular DNA molecules within bacteria that can replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome, often used as vectors in genetic engineering.
A type of retrovirus capable of infecting both dividing and non-dividing cells, commonly used for gene delivery in medical applications.

subsystems.name: Editing machinery
subsystems.role: the molecule that cuts or rewrites DNA at a chosen address.
parts: single-guide RNA that matches the target
base editors (chemical change without a double-strand break)

subsystems.name: Delivery system
subsystems.role: gets the editor into the right cells and nowhere else.
parts: electroporation for cells edited outside the body

subsystems.name: Cell engineering (ex vivo route)
subsystems.role: patient cells are removed, edited, checked and returned.

subsystems.name: Targeting and specificity control
subsystems.role: keeps edits on-target and reversible if needed.

subsystems.name: Manufacturing and quality
subsystems.role: turns lab reagents into injectable medicine.

subsystems.name: Safety and immune monitoring
subsystems.role: manages immune reactions to bacterial editing proteins and long-term effects.

buildSteps.title: Choose the edit
buildSteps.detail: Decide whether to disable a gene, correct a single letter, or insert a sequence — each needs a different tool.

buildSteps.title: Design the guide and editor
buildSteps.detail: Software picks the guide RNA with the best on-target activity and the fewest near-matches elsewhere in the genome.

buildSteps.title: Build the reagents
buildSteps.detail: DNA templates are synthesised, RNA or protein is produced, purified and tested; clinical batches are made under GMP conditions.

buildSteps.title: Deliver the editor
buildSteps.detail: Outside the body, cells are collected and electroporated. Inside the body, lipid nanoparticles or AAV vectors carry the payload, mostly to the liver today.

buildSteps.title: Verify the edit
buildSteps.detail: Deep sequencing measures how many cells were edited and whether any unwanted changes appeared.

buildSteps.title: Expand or dose
buildSteps.detail: For ex vivo therapy, edited cells are grown to a therapeutic dose; for in vivo therapy, the formulated medicine is infused.

buildSteps.title: Monitor the patient
buildSteps.detail: Blood counts, immune reactions and, ideally, a treated disease are tracked for years.

prerequisites.why: the first editing tool reliable enough to use as a medicine.
they avoid cutting both DNA strands, which lowers the risk of scrambled chromosomes.
lipid nanoparticles concentrate in the liver; reaching muscle, brain or lung safely is still unsolved.
editing enzymes and guide RNAs must be made to injectable purity at scale.
no one yet knows the cancer risk of editing many cells in a living patient decades later.

pathway.milestone: the first ex vivo CRISPR therapy approved in late 2023 for sickle cell disease, plus mRNA vaccines proving lipid-nanoparticle delivery
pathway.unlocks: regulatory and manufacturing groundwork for editing as medicine.

pathway.milestone: single-infusion in vivo editing for liver-made proteins, in trials for conditions such as hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis and high cholesterol
pathway.unlocks: treatments for diseases now managed only with lifelong drugs.

pathway.milestone: editing delivered to organs other than the liver

pathway.unlocks: treatments tuned to a patient's own genetics, and engineered immune cells that attack tumours.
